cards.prompt: Street of houses: no two neighbors
cards.setup: House i has cash v[i]. Rob a set of houses with the most cash, never two next to each other.
cards.answer: dp[i] = max(dp[i−1], dp[i−2] + v[i]); dp[0]=0, dp[1]=v[1]; answer dp[n]. Table: 2, 7, 11, 11, 12.
cards.explain: One sequence plus "use some of them" means a prefix state. Split on the last element: in or out.

steps.q: In the best plan for [2, 7, 9, 3, 1], what can happen to the last house?
steps.answer: It is robbed or skipped, and each case leaves a smaller street
steps.why: Two cases. Skipping it leaves houses 1..4. Robbing it forbids house 4 and leaves houses 1..3.
options: It depends on every earlier choice, so list the subsets
It is robbed or skipped, and each case leaves a smaller street
It is always robbed because it adds cash

miss.It is always robbed because it adds cash: Robbing it can block a bigger neighbor. In [3, 10, 1] the best plan skips the last house.
miss.It depends on every earlier choice, so l: Listing subsets is the 2^n brute force. You only need to decide the last house.

steps.q: Which subproblem makes "rob or skip the last house" work?
steps.answer: dp[i] = most cash from houses 1..i
steps.why: Both cases leave a shorter street that starts at house 1, which is just a smaller prefix.
options: dp[i] = most cash robbing exactly i houses
dp[i][j] = most cash from houses i..j

miss.dp[i] = most cash robbing exactly i hous: A count does not say which houses were robbed, so you cannot check neighbors.
miss.dp[i] = v[i]: That is the input, not a subproblem.
miss.dp[i][j] = most cash from houses i..j: This works, but i is always 1, so it wastes a dimension and n² space.

steps.q: Skipping house i leaves dp[i−1]. Robbing house i gives…
steps.answer: dp[i−2] + v[i]
steps.why: Robbing house i forbids house i−1. What is left is houses 1..i−2.
options: max over all j < i of dp[j] + v[i]

miss.dp[i−1] + v[i]: dp[i−1] might already rob house i−1, which is next door.
miss.dp[i−2]: You robbed house i, so add its cash v[i].
miss.max over all j < i of dp[j] + v[i]: This is correct but slower. dp only grows with i, so j = i−2 is always the best choice.

steps.why: With one house and no neighbor to worry about, rob it.

miss.0: That skips the only house even though nothing blocks it.
miss.max(v[1], v[2]): That is dp[2]. It looks at two houses.

steps.answer: i = 2 up to n, answer dp[n], O(n) time
steps.why: dp[i] needs dp[i−1] and dp[i−2], so go left to right. Houses 1..n is the whole street.
options: i = 2 up to n, answer dp[n−1]
i = n down to 2, answer dp[1]
i = 2 up to n, answer dp[n], O(n) time

miss.i = n down to 2, answer dp[1]: Under this definition dp[i] depends on smaller i, so those must be filled first.
miss.i = 2 up to n, answer dp[n−1]: That never considers the last house.

cards.source: New practice problem · steps follow the 5-step method (Reducible, "5 Simple Steps for Solving DP Problems")

cards.prompt: Longest increasing subsequence
cards.setup: Find the longest subsequence (any elements, kept in order) where each element is larger than the one before.
cards.answer: dp[i] = 1 + max{dp[j] : j < i, a[j] < a[i]} (1 if there is no such j); answer max over i of dp[i]. Table: 1, 1, 2, 2, 3.
cards.explain: When the next pick depends on the previous pick, make the subproblem "ends exactly at i." The index remembers the last value.

steps.q: Try dp[i] = LIS within the first i elements. To extend it with a[i], what is missing?
steps.answer: The last value of that subsequence, which dp[i−1] does not record
steps.why: a[i] can be added only if it is larger than the subsequence's last value, and a length alone does not say what that value is.
options: The last value of that subsequence, which dp[i−1] does not record
Nothing: dp[i] = dp[i−1] + 1 when a[i] > a[i−1]

miss.Nothing: dp[i] = dp[i−1] + 1 when a[i] >: The best subsequence need not end at a[i−1]. In [1, 5, 2, 3], the first three give length 2 through 1, 5 or 1, 2. Only 1, 2 can take the 3, and the number 2 does not say which one you have.
miss.Only the length dp[i−1]: The length is exactly what you have, and it is not enough. You need the last value.

steps.answer: dp[i] = longest increasing subsequence that ends at a[i]
steps.why: Now the last value is a[i] itself, so you know exactly what can come next.
options: dp[i] = longest one that starts at a[1]
dp[i][v] = longest in the first i elements whose last value is v
dp[i] = how many increasing subsequences end at a[i]
dp[i] = longest increasing subsequence that ends at a[i]

miss.dp[i] = longest one that starts at a[1]: The best subsequence may skip a[1].
miss.dp[i] = how many increasing subsequences: That counts subsequences. The question asks for the longest length.
miss.dp[i][v] = longest in the first i elemen: This is valid, but values can be huge. "Ends at i" stores the same fact with n states.

steps.q: What can come right before a[i] in that subsequence?
steps.answer: Any j < i with a[j] < a[i]: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j]
steps.why: The element before a[i] can be any earlier, smaller element. If there is none, a[i] starts alone and dp[i] = 1.
options: Any j < i with a[j] < a[i]: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j]

miss.Only j = i−1: Subsequences can skip elements. The previous pick need not be adjacent.
miss.dp[i] = max(dp[i−1], dp[i−1] + 1): That is prefix thinking again. dp[i−1] ends at a[i−1], which may be larger than a[i].

steps.q: Fill dp for [3, 1, 4, 2, 5] in your head:
steps.why: 3 and 1 each start alone. 4 follows 3 or 1, so 2. 2 follows 1, so 2. 5 follows 4 or 2, so 3.

miss.1, 1, 2, 3, 4: 2 cannot follow 4 (it is smaller), so dp at 2 is 1 + dp at 1 = 2.
miss.1, 1, 2, 1, 3: 2 can follow 1 (1 < 2), so it is 2, not 1.
miss.1, 2, 3, 4, 5: 1 is smaller than 3, so it cannot extend 3.

steps.answer: The max of dp[i] over all i, O(n²) total
steps.why: The best subsequence can end anywhere. Each of the n entries scans up to n earlier ones.
options: The max of dp[i] over all i, O(n²) total

miss.dp[n]: That forces the subsequence to end at the last element. In [1, 2, 0], dp[n] = 1 but the answer is 2.

cards.source: New practice problem · steps follow the 5-step method (Reducible, "5 Simple Steps for Solving DP Problems")

cards.prompt: Best contiguous run
cards.setup: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum. Entries can be negative.
cards.answer: dp[i] = max(a[i], dp[i−1] + a[i]); answer max over i of dp[i]. Table: −2, 3, 2, 6, 0, 2.
cards.explain: "Contiguous" means an "ends at i" state. The only choice is to extend the run or start fresh.

steps.answer: dp[i] = best sum of a run ending exactly at i
steps.why: A run that ends at i is either a[i] alone or a run ending at i−1 with a[i] added.
options: dp[i] = best sum of a run ending exactly at i
dp[i] = best run anywhere in the first i

miss.dp[i] = best run anywhere in the first i: That best run may stop well before i, so adding a[i] would leave a gap.
miss.dp[i][j] = sum of a[i..j]: Filling every pair is O(n²) brute force with no reuse.

steps.answer: dp[i] = max(a[i], dp[i−1] + a[i])
steps.why: Either extend the best run ending at i−1, or start a new run at i if that run only hurts.

miss.dp[i] = dp[i−1] + a[i]: This always keeps the old run, even when its sum is negative.
miss.dp[i] = max(dp[i−1], a[i]): dp[i−1] does not end at i, so this breaks the definition.

steps.why: 3 starts fresh (better than 1). Then 2, then 6. −6 drops it to 0. 2 starts fresh or extends 0, giving 2 either way.

miss.−2, 3, 3, 6, 6, 6: That is the best sum seen so far, which answers a different question than "ends at i."
miss.−2, 1, 0, 4, −2, 0: That never starts fresh, so the −2 drags everything down.

steps.answer: max of dp = 6
steps.why: The best run ends at index 4, so take the max over every ending.

miss.dp[n] = 2: That only looks at runs ending at the last element.
miss.9, the sum of the positives: That skips elements, and a subarray must be contiguous.

cards.source: New practice problem · steps follow the 5-step method (Reducible, "5 Simple Steps for Solving DP Problems")

cards.prompt: Paint the houses
cards.setup: Paint n houses red, green or blue. cost[i][c] is the price to paint house i color c. Neighbors cannot share a color. Find the minimum total.
cards.example: H1: R1 G5 B3 · H2: R2 G9 B4 · H3: R3 G1 B6 → best 6
cards.answer: dp[i][c] = cost[i][c] + min over c′ ≠ c of dp[i−1][c′]; answer min over c of dp[n][c]. Rows: (1,5,3), (5,10,5), (8,6,11).
cards.explain: If the recurrence needs a fact about the previous choice, add that fact as an index. A state that is too small gets stuck, so add a parameter.

steps.q: Try dp[i] = cheapest way to paint houses 1..i. Why does the recurrence get stuck?
steps.answer: Choosing house i's color needs house i−1's color, and dp[i−1] does not store it
steps.why: The cheapest plan for houses 1..i−1 might end in the color you want for house i.
options: It does not: dp[i] = dp[i−1] + the cheapest color for house i
Choosing house i's color needs house i−1's color, and dp[i−1] does not store it
There are too many subsets of houses

miss.It does not: dp[i] = dp[i−1] + the cheap: That cheapest color may match house i−1. In the example, picking R1 then R2 breaks the rule.
miss.There are too many subsets of houses: You paint every house. The trouble is the colors, not choosing houses.

steps.answer: dp[i][c] = cheapest houses 1..i with house i painted c
steps.why: Now the last color is in the index, so you can rule out matching it.
options: dp[i][c] = cheapest houses 1..i with house i painted c
dp[i][S] for every set S of colors used so far
dp[c] = cost of painting every house c

miss.dp[i][c] = cost[i][c]: That is input, with no subproblem behind it.
miss.dp[i][S] for every set S of colors used: Only the last color matters, so the set is extra state you do not need.

steps.answer: cost[i][c] + min over c′ ≠ c of dp[i−1][c′]
steps.why: House i−1 can be any color except c.
options: cost[i][c] + min over all c′ of dp[i−1][c′]
cost[i][c] + min over c′ ≠ c of dp[i−1][c′]

miss.cost[i][c] + min over all c′ of dp[i−1][: That allows c′ = c, so two neighbors match.
miss.cost[i][c] + dp[i−1][c]: That forces the same color as the neighbor, which is exactly what is forbidden.

steps.answer: 6 (Blue, Red, Green: 3 + 2 + 1)

miss.4 (Red, Red, Green): Houses 1 and 2 are both red, and neighbors cannot match.
miss.8: That is dp[3][Red]. The answer is the min over all colors of the last house.

steps.answer: 3n states, O(1) each, so O(n) total
steps.why: Each state checks 2 earlier colors. With k colors it would be O(nk²).
options: 3n states, O(1) each, so O(n) total

miss.O(3^n): That is trying every coloring. DP avoids it by remembering only the last color.
miss.O(n²): No state looks back further than i−1.

cards.source: New practice problem · steps follow the 5-step method (Reducible, "5 Simple Steps for Solving DP Problems")

cards.prompt: Decode the digits
cards.setup: Letters were encoded as A=1 … Z=26. Count the ways to decode a digit string. "0" alone is not a letter.
cards.explain: Counting adds the separate last-choice cases. The empty prefix has exactly 1 decoding, so dp[0] = 1.

steps.q: In any decoding of the first i digits, the last letter came from…
steps.answer: Either the last 1 digit or the last 2 digits
steps.why: Each letter uses 1 or 2 digits, so there are two cases for the last letter.
options: Either the last 1 digit or the last 2 digits

miss.Always the last 1 digit: "26" can decode as Z, which uses two digits.
miss.Any suffix of the string: No letter uses more than two digits.

steps.answer: dp[i] = number of ways to decode the first i digits
steps.why: Both cases leave a shorter prefix, either i−1 or i−2 digits.
options: dp[i] = can the first i digits be decoded?
dp[i] = number of letters in a decoding of i digits
dp[i] = number of ways to decode the first i digits

miss.dp[i] = can the first i digits be decode: A yes/no loses the count, and the question asks how many.
miss.dp[i] = number of letters in a decoding: Different decodings use different numbers of letters, and that does not count anything.

steps.answer: Add: dp[i−1] (if valid) + dp[i−2] (if valid)
steps.why: Every decoding falls into exactly one case, so the counts add.

miss.max(dp[i−1], dp[i−2]): Max is for optimizing. Counting adds the cases.
miss.dp[i−1] · dp[i−2]: You multiply independent choices made one after another. These are two alternatives.

steps.answer: 1, since the empty string has one decoding (nothing)
steps.why: For "26", dp[2] = dp[1] + dp[0] = 1 + 1 = 2. That checks out.
options: 1, since the empty string has one decoding (nothing)

miss.0: With dp[0] = 0, "26" gets only 1 way, which loses Z.

steps.why: dp = 1, 1, 2, 1, 1. A "0" must pair with the 1 before it (10), so 2|10|1 is the only decoding.

miss.2: 21|0|1 fails because 0 alone is not a letter. 2|1|01 fails because 01 is not a letter.
miss.3: Count the decodings with no lone 0 and no leading-zero pair. Only 2|10|1 works.

cards.source: New practice problem · steps follow the 5-step method (Reducible, "5 Simple Steps for Solving DP Problems")

cards.prompt: Cheapest path through a grid
cards.setup: From the top-left to the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down. Minimize the sum of cells visited.
cards.answer: dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r−1][c], dp[r][c−1]); first row and column are running sums; answer dp[last][last].
cards.explain: On a grid the state is the position. Split on the last move into the cell.

steps.q: The last move into the bottom-right cell came from…
steps.answer: The cell above or the cell to the left
steps.why: Only right and down moves are allowed, so there are two cases.
options: The cell above or the cell to the left

miss.Any neighbor: Up and left moves are not allowed.

steps.answer: dp[r][c] = cheapest path from the start to cell (r, c)
steps.why: Each case leaves a cheapest path to a neighboring cell, which is the same kind of question.
options: dp[r] = cheapest cell in row r
dp[k] = cheapest path of k steps
dp[r][c] = cheapest path from the start to cell (r, c)

miss.dp[k] = cheapest path of k steps: Many cells are k steps away, so this does not say where you are.
miss.dp[r] = cheapest cell in row r: Paths are not made of the cheapest cell in each row.

steps.answer: grid[r][c] + min(dp[r−1][c], dp[r][c−1])
steps.why: Pay for this cell, plus the cheaper of the two ways in.

miss.min(dp[r−1][c], dp[r][c−1]): This forgets to pay for the cell itself.

steps.answer: First row and first column are running sums
steps.why: Those cells have only one way in, from the left or from above.
options: First row and first column are running sums

miss.All 0: You still pay for those cells.
miss.Only dp[0][0] is needed: Cells on the edge would look up a neighbor that does not exist.

steps.answer: Row by row, left to right
steps.why: Each cell needs the one above it and the one to its left, and both are done by then. The answer is 7.
options: Row by row, left to right

miss.Bottom-right back to top-left: That order fits the other definition (cheapest path from a cell to the end). With start-to-cell, the cells it depends on are not filled yet.
miss.Any order works: Only top-down memoization can ignore order. A table must be filled in dependency order.

cards.source: New practice problem · steps follow the 5-step method (Reducible, "5 Simple Steps for Solving DP Problems")

cards.prompt: Split into words
cards.setup: Can string s be split into dictionary words, with words allowed to repeat?
cards.answer: dp[i] = OR over j < i of (dp[j] AND s[j+1..i] is a word); dp[0] = true; answer dp[n].
cards.explain: When the last piece can be any length, the recurrence loops over where it starts.

steps.q: In a valid split of the first i letters, the last word is…
steps.answer: Some word ending at i, starting anywhere
steps.why: Words have different lengths, so try every start j+1.
options: The longest dictionary word that fits
Some word ending at i, starting anywhere

miss.The longest dictionary word that fits: Greedy fails here: "cats" leaves "and", which is not a word, but cat|sand works.
miss.Exactly the last letter: Words are usually longer than one letter.

steps.answer: dp[i] = can the first i letters be split?
steps.why: Removing the last word leaves a shorter prefix, the same question.
options: dp[i] = does a word start at letter i?
dp[i] = can the first i letters be split?

miss.dp[i] = does a word start at letter i?: That describes one spot, not whether the whole prefix splits.
miss.One entry per dictionary word: The string is what gets shorter, not the dictionary.

steps.answer: OR over j of (dp[j] AND s[j+1..i] is a word)
steps.why: One valid split is enough, so ask whether any last word works.
options: dp[i−1] AND s[i] is a word
OR over j of (dp[j] AND s[j+1..i] is a word)

miss.AND over j of (…): That would require every possible split to work.

steps.answer: true
steps.why: The empty prefix is trivially split, and it lets the first word count.

miss.false: Then every OR is false and nothing could ever be split.

cards.source: New practice problem · steps follow the 5-step method (Reducible, "5 Simple Steps for Solving DP Problems")

cards.prompt: Fewest insertions to a palindrome
cards.setup: Insert letters anywhere in s to make it a palindrome. Find the minimum number of insertions.
cards.answer: dp[i][j] = s[i]=s[j] ? dp[i+1][j−1] : 1 + min(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j−1]); length ≤ 1 → 0; fill by increasing length; answer dp[1][n].
cards.explain: When both ends matter (palindromes, taking from either end, merging), use intervals i..j and fill them by length.

steps.q: Look at the two ends of s[i..j]. What is the case split?
steps.answer: Equal ends pair up; otherwise one end gets a new partner inserted
steps.why: If s[i] = s[j], only the middle is left. If not, insert a copy of one end next to the other side and solve what remains.
options: Equal ends pair up; otherwise one end gets a new partner inserted

miss.Only the last letter matters: A palindrome compares both ends, so the first letter matters just as much.
miss.Delete the last letter: You can only insert, not delete.

steps.answer: dp[i][j] = fewest insertions for s[i..j]
steps.why: Every case trims one or both ends, so what remains is always an interval.
options: dp[i][j] = 1 if s[i..j] is a palindrome, else 0
dp[i] = fewest insertions for the prefix s[1..i]

miss.dp[i] = fewest insertions for the prefix: Trimming the left end breaks the prefix.

steps.why: One insertion matches one end, and the rest of the interval is still to solve.

miss.1 + dp[i+1][j−1]: That fixes both ends with one change, which is a substitution, not an insertion.
miss.2 + dp[i+1][j−1]: This is valid but never better than the min above, so it is not the recurrence.

steps.answer: By increasing interval length
steps.why: Each interval needs shorter intervals inside it. The answer is dp[1][n]. That is n² states at O(1) each.
options: Left to right by j only
i from 1 up to n, then j from i up to n

miss.i from 1 up to n, then j from i up to n: dp[i][j] needs dp[i+1][·], and that row would not be filled yet.
miss.Left to right by j only: That is two indices squeezed into one. The table is 2D.

cards.source: New practice problem · steps follow the 5-step method (Reducible, "5 Simple Steps for Solving DP Problems")

cards.prompt: Facing a new DP problem: what are the 5 steps?
cards.answer: 1 Visualize a tiny example and spot the last decision. 2 Name the subproblem in words. 3 Relate it to smaller subproblems, one case per option of that last decision. 4 Generalize: base cases and the full recurrence. 5 Order: fill smaller first, then say where the answer lives.
cards.explain: Step 2 is where problems are won. If step 3 gets stuck because you need a fact the subproblem does not hold, go back to step 2 and add that fact as an index.
cards.source: Subproblem shapes · study answer checked against the Quiz 5 lessons

cards.prompt: How do you test a subproblem before writing the recurrence?
cards.answer: Three checks: the original problem is one of them (or the best of them); each one is solved by one last decision plus smaller ones; there are only polynomially many.
cards.explain: Say it in words first, like "dp[i] = the best total using only the first i houses." If you cannot say what one entry means, the recurrence will not come.
cards.source: Subproblem shapes · study answer checked against the Quiz 5 lessons

cards.prompt: Input shape → first subproblem to try?
cards.answer: One sequence: prefix dp[i]. Two sequences: dp[i][j] over both prefixes. Budget or capacity: add the remaining budget as an index. Must link to the previous pick, or contiguous: ends exactly at i. Both ends matter: interval dp[i][j]. Grid: the cell (r, c).
cards.explain: These are starting guesses, not rules. Each one keeps the fact the next decision needs.
cards.source: Subproblem shapes · study answer checked against the Quiz 5 lessons

cards.prompt: One list of numbers. Pick some to maximize the sum, never two neighbors. First subproblem to try?
cards.answer: dp[i] = best using the first i numbers
cards.explain: Prefixes shrink cleanly: the last number is either picked or not, and each case leaves a smaller prefix.
options: dp[i] = best using the first i numbers
Try every subset and keep the best
dp[i] = best using exactly i numbers

miss.dp[i] = best using exactly i numbers: A count does not say which numbers were used, so you cannot check the no-neighbors rule.
miss.dp[i][j] = best using numbers i..j: This works, but the left end is always 1, so the extra index is wasted.
miss.Try every subset and keep the best: That is the 2^n brute force DP is meant to replace.

cards.prompt: Two strings. You compare or align them letter by letter. Subproblem?
cards.answer: dp[i][j] over the first i of one and the first j of the other
cards.explain: The last decision touches the end of one or both strings, so you need a position in each. LCS and edit distance both work this way.
options: dp[i][j] over the first i of one and the first j of the other
dp[i] = do the strings match up to i?
dp[i] over the first i letters of the longer string

miss.dp[i] over the first i letters of the lo: This forgets where you are in the other string, and the answer depends on both.
miss.dp[i] = do the strings match up to i?: A yes/no for one shared index cannot hold insertions, which shift one string against the other.

cards.prompt: Items with weights, each used at most once, total weight ≤ W. Why is dp[i] (first i items) not enough?
cards.answer: Same i, different remaining capacity → different answers
cards.explain: Whether item i fits depends on how much room is left, so the capacity must be an index: dp[i][w].
options: You need dp[w] only, with no items index
It is enough; take the item if it fits
Same i, different remaining capacity → different answers

miss.It is enough; take the item if it fits: Fitting is not the question. Taking item i can block better items, and dp[i] cannot compare those cases.
miss.You need dp[w] only, with no items index: Without i you cannot stop an item being used twice. The 1D trick works only because of a careful reverse loop.

cards.prompt: Unlimited copies of each coin or piece. Smallest useful subproblem?
cards.answer: dp[a] = best for the remaining amount a
cards.explain: Using a coin leaves the same choices as before, just for a smaller amount. Only the amount changes.
options: dp[a] = best for the remaining amount a

miss.dp[i][a] is required: This also works, but with unlimited reuse the amount alone describes what is left.
miss.dp[k] = best using k coins: Knowing how many coins you used does not tell you how much is left to make.

cards.prompt: Longest subsequence where each pick must be larger than the previous pick. Subproblem?
cards.answer: dp[i] = best that ends exactly at element i
cards.explain: To add element i you must know the previous pick's value. "Ends at j" puts that value, a[j], in the index.
options: dp[i] = best within the first i elements
dp[i] = best that starts at element 1
dp[i] = best that ends exactly at element i

miss.dp[i] = best within the first i elements: The best within the prefix might end on a huge value, so you cannot tell whether a[i] extends it.

cards.prompt: Best contiguous subarray or substring. Subproblem?
cards.answer: dp[i] = best that ends exactly at i
cards.explain: Contiguous means the only thing you can extend is a piece ending at i−1. So extend it or start fresh at i.
options: dp[i] = best anywhere in the first i
dp[i] = best that ends exactly at i
dp[i][j] = sum of i..j for every pair

miss.dp[i] = best anywhere in the first i: The best piece so far may stop far from i, and then extending it would leave a gap.
miss.dp[i][j] = sum of i..j for every pair: That is O(n²) entries with no reuse, really just brute force in a table.

cards.prompt: The rule involves both ends at once, as in palindromes, removing from either end, or merging neighbors. Subproblem?
cards.answer: Interval dp[i][j] for the piece i..j
cards.explain: Each step removes the left end, the right end, or both, so what remains is always a contiguous interval.
options: Interval dp[i][j] for the piece i..j

miss.Prefix dp[i]: Removing from the left end of a prefix leaves something that is not a prefix.
miss.Suffix dp[i]: Same problem on the other side. Removing from the right end of a suffix breaks it.

cards.prompt: Your recurrence needs to know the previous color, whether you hold a stock, or the last item taken. Fix?
cards.answer: Add that fact as another index
cards.explain: For example dp[i][c] means "first i houses, house i painted c." The state must hold everything the next decision depends on.
options: Add that fact as another index
Store the whole history of choices

miss.Switch to greedy: Greedy needs its own exchange proof, and it is usually wrong exactly when the state is missing something.
miss.Store the whole history of choices: Histories grow exponentially. Keep only the one fact the next step needs.

cards.source: Subproblem shapes · study answer checked against the Quiz 5 lessons

cards.prompt: You have one case per option of the last decision. How do you combine them?
cards.answer: max/min to optimize, + to count, OR for yes/no
cards.explain: The cases split the possible solutions into separate groups. Take the best group, add up the groups, or ask whether any group works.
options: max/min to optimize, + to count, OR for yes/no

miss.Always max: Counting decodings or paths adds the cases. Taking a max undercounts.
miss.Multiply the cases: Multiplying is for independent choices made one after another. Here the cases are alternatives.

cards.source: Subproblem shapes · study answer checked against the Quiz 5 lessons

cards.prompt: Where is the final answer?
cards.answer: Prefix: dp[n]. Ends-at-i: the max over all i.
cards.explain: A prefix state for n already covers the whole input. An "ends at i" state fixes the ending, so you have to check every ending.
options: Prefix: dp[n]. Ends-at-i: the max over all i.

miss.Always dp[n]: With "ends at i" the best answer may end earlier. In [1, 2, 0] the longest increasing run ends at index 2, not 3.
miss.Always dp[0] or dp[1]: Those are base cases, the smallest subproblems, not the full problem.

cards.source: Subproblem shapes · study answer checked against the Quiz 5 lessons

cards.prompt: What is a DP state?
cards.answer: A complete description of one subproblem.
cards.explain: It contains everything that can change the answer or the legal next choices.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Top-down DP stores answers during…
cards.answer: Recursion
cards.explain: Memoization computes a requested state recursively, then caches its result.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: What is tabulation?
cards.answer: Compute states in dependency order.
cards.explain: Bottom-up DP initializes base cases and computes larger states only after their dependencies.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Why does Fibonacci benefit from caching?
cards.answer: The recursive branches repeat states.
cards.explain: A cached non-base answer avoids recomputing its whole subtree.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.explain: The sequence is 0,1,1,2,3,5,8.
cards.math: F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2)F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2)F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2)
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Optimal value versus witness: what is the difference?
cards.answer: A score versus the actual choices.
cards.explain: A knapsack value of 7 is a number; items 1 and 2 are a witness. Traceback recovers choices.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: What does C(a) mean in minimum coin change?
cards.answer: Fewest coins making exactly amount a.
cards.explain: Coins are positive integers, with unlimited copies. Impossible states use infinity.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Which initialization is correct?
cards.answer: C(0)=0; unreachable amounts=∞
cards.explain: An unreachable amount must not look like a free solution.
cards.math: C(0)=0C(0)=0C(0)=0
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Coins {1,3,4}, amount 6. Minimum?
cards.explain: 3+3 beats greedy 4+1+1.
cards.math: C(6)=min⁡(3,2,3)=2C(6)=\min(3,2,3)=2C(6)=min(3,2,3)=2
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Coins {3,4}, amount 5. Result?
cards.answer: Impossible
cards.explain: Neither 3 nor 4 leaves a reachable remainder. Store infinity.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Why fill coin amounts upward?
cards.answer: Every dependency a−d is smaller than a.
cards.explain: Strictly positive denominations ensure the table dependency order and recursive termination.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: For {1,3,4}, target 6: traceback emits 3. Next amount?
cards.explain: Subtract the chosen denomination: 6−3=3. Then another 3 reaches 0.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Should a memo cache impossible results?
cards.answer: Yes
cards.explain: Otherwise impossible states can be recomputed repeatedly. Test cache membership, not whether its value is truthy.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Target 0: what is the witness?
cards.answer: An empty list of coins.
cards.explain: No coins are needed; this is a valid reachable base case.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: What does K(i,c) mean?
cards.answer: Best value with the first i items, weight at most c.
cards.explain: The item prefix prevents reusing an item. This is an at-most-capacity model.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Taking item i reads which row?
cards.explain: The chosen item cannot remain available. Both skip and take branches use the previous row.
cards.math: vi+K(i−1,c−wi)v_i+K(i-1,c-w_i)vi​+K(i−1,c−wi​)
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.explain: Take the first two items: weight 2+3=5 and value 3+4=7.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: One item (weight 2, value 3), capacity 4. 0/1 optimum?
cards.explain: There is only one copy. Returning 6 accidentally solves an unlimited-copy variant.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: One-array 0/1 DP: loop capacity…
cards.answer: Downward
cards.explain: Then the smaller capacity still represents the previous item prefix, preventing reuse.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: K(i,c) equals the cell above. Must item i be taken?
cards.answer: No; skipping preserves an optimum.
cards.explain: A tie may also allow taking, but choosing to skip returns one optimal witness.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Item weight exceeds capacity. What do you do?
cards.answer: Copy K(i−1,c).
cards.explain: The take branch is infeasible; only skipping remains.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Does a subsequence have to be contiguous?
cards.answer: No; order matters, gaps are allowed.
cards.explain: A substring is contiguous. Mixing these definitions changes the problem.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: LCS last characters match. Which recurrence?
cards.answer: 1 + diagonal
cards.explain: Append the shared character to an optimum for the two shorter prefixes.
cards.math: L(i,j)=1+L(i−1,j−1)L(i,j)=1+L(i-1,j-1)L(i,j)=1+L(i−1,j−1)
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: LCS last characters differ. Which recurrence?
cards.answer: max(top,left)
cards.explain: At least one final character must be excluded; consider both cases.
cards.math: L(i,j)=max⁡(L(i−1,j),L(i,j−1))L(i,j)=\max(L(i-1,j),L(i,j-1))L(i,j)=max(L(i−1,j),L(i,j−1))
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: AGGCT and AGCATA: LCS length?
cards.explain: AGCT is a common subsequence of length 4; the official table agrees.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: AB versus BA: give one LCS.
cards.answer: A or B
cards.explain: Both have optimal length 1. A tie can lead to more than one valid witness.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Why reverse characters collected during LCS traceback?
cards.answer: Traceback visits the last character first.
cards.explain: You walk from the final state toward empty prefixes, so the output is accumulated backwards.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: One prefix is empty. What is its LCS length?
cards.explain: No characters can be shared with an empty string.
cards.math: L(0,j)=L(i,0)=0L(0,j)=L(i,0)=0L(0,j)=L(i,0)=0
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Empty source → ABC: edit distance?
cards.explain: Insert A, B and C. Edit-distance boundaries count remaining characters.
cards.math: D(0,j)=jD(0,j)=jD(0,j)=j
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Edit-distance last characters match. Cost?
cards.answer: Diagonal, with no extra cost.
cards.explain: A match consumes both characters without an edit.
cards.math: D(i,j)=D(i−1,j−1)D(i,j)=D(i-1,j-1)D(i,j)=D(i−1,j−1)
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: In prefix edit distance, the left neighbor corresponds to…
cards.answer: Insertion
cards.explain: D(i,j−1) transforms the source prefix into the shorter target; insert B[j].
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: kitten → sitting: minimum unit-cost edits?
cards.explain: Substitute k→s; substitute e→i; insert g. The second edit is a substitution.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Edit traceback stops when…
cards.answer: Both prefix indices reach zero.
cards.explain: If just one is zero, the other prefix still requires deletions or insertions.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Substitution cost becomes 2. What changes?
cards.answer: Only its candidate cost becomes 2+diagonal.
cards.explain: Insertion/deletion remain 1+left and 1+above. A match still costs 0.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: How do you justify a DP recurrence?
cards.answer: Cover every optimum and show every candidate is feasible.
cards.explain: Then use induction in a dependency-respecting order to justify the table algorithm.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Before filling C(a), what is the invariant?
cards.answer: All smaller nonnegative amounts already have correct values.
cards.explain: Positive coin values make every accessed a−d smaller than a.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: One dimension means linear time. True?
cards.answer: False
cards.explain: Coin change has V amounts but k coin choices per amount, giving Θ(kV).
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Why is O(nW) knapsack pseudo-polynomial?
cards.answer: W is a numeric magnitude, not its bit length.
cards.explain: A W encoded in b bits can be as large as about 2^b.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: abc needs how many insertions to be a palindrome?
cards.explain: abcba uses two insertions. No single insertion makes abc a palindrome.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Fewest perfect squares summing to 12?
cards.explain: 4+4+4 uses 3 squares. No two squares add to 12.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Recall coin change: state, base, recurrence, cost.
cards.answer: C(a): fewest coins for exact a. C(0)=0.
cards.explain: Infinity means impossible; k denominations, target V. Time Θ(kV), space Θ(V).
cards.math: C(a)=min⁡d≤a{1+C(a−d)}C(a)=\min_{d\le a}\{1+C(a-d)\}C(a)=d≤amin​{1+C(a−d)}
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Recall the 0/1 take-or-skip recurrence.
cards.answer: max(skip, take from previous row)
cards.explain: Use positive weights and at-most capacity. Time/space Θ(nW) for the full table.
cards.math: skip=K(i−1,c)take=vi+K(i−1,c−wi)K(i,c)=max⁡(skip,take)\begin{aligned}\text{skip}&=K(i-1,c)\\\text{take}&=v_i+K(i-1,c-w_i)\\K(i,c)&=\max(\text{skip},\text{take})\end{aligned}skiptakeK(i,c)​=K(i−1,c)=vi​+K(i−1,c−wi​)=max(skip,take)​
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Recall LCS boundaries and transitions.
cards.answer: Empty prefix = 0; match = 1+diagonal; mismatch = max(top,left).
cards.explain: Time/space Θ(mn) for full table. Traceback O(m+n).

cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Recall edit-distance boundaries and transitions.
cards.answer: Empty source = j; empty target = i; match = diagonal.
cards.explain: Mismatch adds 1 to min(left,top,diagonal). Time/space Θ(mn).

cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Recall the runtime rule.
cards.answer: Number of states × work per state.
cards.explain: Add reconstruction separately. Table dimensions alone do not capture all work.
cards.math: T=#states×work per stateT=\#\text{states}\times\text{work per state}T=#states×work per state
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer

cards.prompt: Traceback costs: coin, knapsack, string DPs?
cards.answer: O(number of coins), O(n), O(m+n).
cards.explain: These are additional to building the full value tables. Output memory is separate.
cards.source: Chapter 5 concepts; independently checked study answer
